title: University of Paris Condemns 28 Magical Propositions
description:
In 1398 the Faculty of Theology of the University of Paris issued a formal condemnation of twenty-eight propositions relating to magic, divination, and demonic pact. The document, drawn up in response to growing concern about the spread of magical practice among educated elites, systematically defined the theological boundaries between licit and illicit engagement with supernatural powers. Among the condemned propositions were the belief that demons could be compelled by ritual, that divinatory arts reliably produced true knowledge, and that explicit or implicit pacts with demons were compatible with Christian faith.

The Paris condemnation represents a crucial moment of institutional consolidation in the theological treatment of magic. By articulating clear doctrinal boundaries and explicitly connecting diverse magical practices to the principle of demonic compact, the Faculty provided intellectual infrastructure for the developing theory of witchcraft. The cumulative concept of witchcraft — combining heresy, apostasy, and magical harm through a unifying principle of diabolical pact — required exactly this kind of authoritative theological statement to give it procedural traction in ecclesiastical courts.

The document was widely disseminated and cited by later demonologists including Jean Gerson, who had participated in the deliberations. Its influence extended through the fifteenth century, appearing in works that directly preceded the Malleus Maleficarum. The Paris condemnation thus marks a point at which university theology, inquisitorial practice, and pastoral concern converged to produce a systematic framework for identifying, prosecuting, and punishing those accused of demonic compact.
historiographical_note: Michael Bailey's Battling Demons: Witchcraft, Heresy, and Reform in the Late Middle Ages (2003) situates the Paris condemnation within a broader fifteenth-century reform movement that connected magical practice to social disorder. Richard Kieckhefer's Magic in the Middle Ages (1990) provides essential context for understanding the intellectual traditions the Paris theologians were systematizing.
source_method: Published theological documents; secondary scholarship on late medieval magic and demonology
